value.The claims surge: In the moderate scenario 0.67 million workers are displaced by 2035-36 and recipients of replaced payments rise by 0.95 million, 93% of the JobSeeker group's stock; in the severe scenario 1.77 million and 2.53 million (248%). The model's inflow is about 164,000 newly displaced workers a year over 2032-33 to 2035-36 in the moderate scenario (159,000 to 173,000) and 437,000 in the severe (425,000 to 462,000): 0.7 to 0.8 and 1.9 to 2.1 times the baseline flow of retrenchments, and about 0.32 to 0.35 and 0.86 to 0.95 times the JobSeeker claims Services Australia granted a year in 2023-24 to 2025-26 (510,000 to 462,000; a further 77,600 to 80,000 Youth Allowance jobseekers). Claims took a mean of 22 days (JobSeeker) and 26 (Youth Allowance) in 2023-24; in the 2020 surge 1.07 million claims were finalised in eight weeks at a mean of 10 days with payroll-data automation, the precedent for a surge protocol. Under current rules the liquid-assets waiting period (from A$5,500 single or A$11,000 partnered, up to 13 weeks) and the assets test (A$333,000 single homeowner to A$766,000 non-homeowner couple) would delay or deny payment to displaced workers with savings or non-home property; no asset microdata is available to count them. The partner income test removes 31% of displaced households from any payment on the floor and 37% under the status quo; 62% are couples.
value.Debt service on the floor: Of the 0.66 million households with a displaced worker in the moderate scenario, 0.35 million have a mortgage and 0.22 million rent privately. On the floor, 210 thousand mortgage holders pay more than 30% of their remaining household income in repayments and 63 thousand more than half (status quo: 222 and 85 thousand); among private renters 159 thousand pay more than 30% in rent on the floor and 156 thousand with P*'s Rent Assistance (status quo 168 thousand). In the severe scenario the mortgage counts are 546 and 168 thousand on the floor. About 40% of loans had under three months of repayments in buffers in 2022 (over half of them fixed-rate or investor loans) and the median buffer was over a year in October 2026; on that share about 25 thousand of the moderate scenario's 63 thousand would exhaust their buffers within three months. Mortgage non-performing loans were 1.01% of credit in June 2026 (peak 1.11% in June 2020); hardship arrangements usually run up to three months, and after serious arrears the median is three months to repayment and six to cure or foreclosure.
value.Forced sales and asset prices: As a stress test, if the 63 thousand displaced mortgage holders above half their income on the floor (status quo 85 thousand; severe scenario 168 thousand) all sold within a year, they would add 11.3% (moderate) or 30.1% (severe) to the 560,005 dwelling transfers recorded in 2025-26 (11.7% and 31.2% of the five-year average). The national price effect is not quantified: no Australian evidence converts extra forced sales into a national price fall, and the local evidence (a 27% foreclosure discount and about 1% lower nearby prices in Massachusetts; −0.9% per extra concurrent listing within 250 m in Blacktown) describes an effect that is local and concentrated where displaced workers live, not a national index; the only imported benchmark, the United States crisis finding that 10% more homes on the market went with prices about 4 points lower, is not transferable. The model has no asset-price feedback: stamp duty and land tax are state taxes outside it (A$34.4bn and A$20.0bn in 2024-25; in NSW a point of prices is worth A$122m of duty and a point of volumes A$98m, so forced sales and a price fall pull state receipts in opposite directions), and the five taxes feel a price fall only through the excess profits tax, whose bank share the PBO costing does not disclose; at 90% of its yield P*'s first levy moves to 2032-33 and its levies to A$124bn. Whether rents rise or fall is not established. The floor cuts the status quo's count of mortgage holders above the 50% line by about 25%, because most displaced mortgage holders have a working partner whose earnings matter more than the payment; Rent Assistance helps only renters.
value.Policy responses: Automatically enrolling displaced workers from Single Touch Payroll data would cost A$4.3bn a year in the moderate scenario and A$11.4bn in the severe, by 2035-36 (the extra take-up on the surge only, at the floor); the 2020 surge shows the machinery exists. Waiving the liquid-assets waiting period for displaced workers would cost at most A$1.6bn to A$4.2bn a year during the inflow, less in proportion to the share actually subject to it. Deferring the assets test on investment property, and a mortgage hardship protocol, cannot be priced by the model.

value.P* re-costed: P* as first printed was not at Part 1 alone's budget: on the fiscal model's own basis it cost A$6.2bn more in 2028-29, because its child payment was costed against the household model's higher current FTB and was not charged its prior-year timing cost. Re-costed at Part 1's cost, P* pays A$6,750 a child a year (Part 1's supplement is A$7,452) and keeps the floor and Rent Assistance +75%.
value.Poverty: At the same cost as Part 1, P* cuts poverty after housing costs to 10.5% on the relative line, against 11.3% for Part 1 and 9.0% for the targeted package: 0.20 million fewer people in poverty than Part 1, and 0.40 million more than the package. Child poverty is 6.6% (Part 1 7.2%), sole-parent households 14.8% (16.4%) and people aged 67 and over 11.6% (12.1%).
value.Robustness: Across 9 household-model configurations (three random seeds and three calibrations), P* has less poverty than Part 1 in every group shown and a higher first-year net benefit in every one (A$0.8bn to A$3.1bn a year on the complete accounting); the targeted package has less poverty than P* in every group in every configuration.
value.Cost and borrowing: P* costs A$62.0bn in 2028-29 (1.86% of GDP), rising to A$130.8bn in 2045-46. The five taxes fall A$20.7bn short in the first year; that is borrowing, repaid with interest by 30 June 2032. Surpluses then build to A$45bn and are drawn down from the late 2030s.
value.The levy: On central yields a levy is first needed in 2043-44 (in 2044-45 if Rent Assistance grows on the fiscal model's path rather than with the model's rents), totalling A$37bn to 2045-46 and peaking at 0.62% of market income; Part 1's is 2044-45 and A$26bn. The five taxes must yield 100.2% of their costings for no levy before 2044-45.
value.Stress test: Drawing tax yield, behavioural responses, cost overruns, the household calibration and the AI path together, the chance of a levy before 2044-45 is 74% for P* (73% for Part 1) and before 2034-35 59% (58%); with symmetric uncertainty alone it is 48% and 37%. The most likely first levy year is 2032-33, when an advance not repaid by then would be levied at once. P* carries the same funding risk as Part 1; the package carries more.
value.A phased start: Starting the floor and Rent Assistance in 2028-29 and the child payment a year later removes the first-year borrowing: 2028-29 costs A$24.8bn against A$41.3bn of taxes, and on central yields no levy is needed to 2045-46. The price is a year without the child payment: A$26.4bn of family payments above the FTB families keep (a budget saving of A$37.3bn).
value.After housing costs: The no-worse-off rule protects payments under today's rules, not income after housing costs. In the paper's rent and interest-rate scenario, 1.11 million households on current payments (2.30 million people) are worse off under Part 1, by about A$933 a year; under P* 0.70 million (1.65 million people, about A$770): mostly Disability Support Pension households (0.28 million) and Age Pension households that own or are buying their home (0.26 million), whom Rent Assistance does not reach.
value.Poverty after the housing scenario: After the scenario's rent and interest-rate effects (central case), poverty on the relative line is 11.1% with P*, 11.7% with Part 1 and 9.8% with the package.
value.Who is better off after the taxes: Before the funding taxes 62% of households gain from P*; after them 35% are better off (33% by A$5 a week or more), against 33% under Part 1 and 42% under the package.
value.Net benefit: On the paper's complete accounting every design's first-year net benefit is negative at its 1.5 to 2.0 weights; it breaks even at a weight of 2.3 to 4.9 on gains to households in poverty for P* (2.8 to 6.1 for Part 1, 2.0 to 3.8 for the package). With the Green Book's standard weights every design is positive: P* A$40bn to A$49bn, Part 1 A$37bn to A$46bn, the package A$51bn to A$60bn, so standard weights widen the package's lead.
value.The trial's work-effort cap: At OpenResearch's revised 3.9-point fall in participation, the Australian trial would trip the 3-point cap with probability 0.79 to 0.84 (0.86 to 0.91 at 4.2). The costed labour response, 16 cents a dollar, is an income response and stays.
